claims.text: The baseline binder-based additive-manufacturing process uses ambient-air debinding followed by solid-state sintering.
Baseline components exhibit dimensional inaccuracies and mechanical defects.
Oxidation and incomplete binder removal contribute to the baseline dimensional inaccuracies and mechanical defects.
Ambient-air debinding should be replaced by high-vacuum debinding before solid-state sintering.
Debinding should use the baseline temperature profile at a pressure below 10^-3 Torr, followed by the same sintering parameters as the baseline.
High-vacuum debinding reduces oxidation relative to ambient-air debinding.
High-vacuum debinding produces more uniform binder removal than ambient-air debinding.
Reduced oxidation and more uniform binder removal lead to fewer microstructural defects.
Reduced oxidation and more uniform binder removal improve densification during subsequent sintering.
Vacuum minimizes oxygen exposure and therefore reduces oxidation of alloy constituents.
Vacuum debinding prevents formation of oxide layers and carbon residues that can act as defect sites.
Vacuum debinding facilitates controlled grain growth during sintering.
Vacuum-debound components will have tighter dimensional tolerances than ambient-air-debound components.
Vacuum-debound components will have higher mechanical strength than ambient-air-debound components.
Vacuum-debound components will have improved toughness relative to ambient-air-debound components.
The predicted dimensional and mechanical improvements arise from fewer defect sites and a more homogeneous microstructure.
The intervention applies when oxidation during debinding is a significant contributor to defects in binder-based additively manufactured high-entropy alloys.
The intervention may not improve alloys or binder systems that are inherently resistant to oxidation under ambient debinding conditions.
The optimal vacuum level and debinding profile vary with alloy composition and binder formulation.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in both dimensional precision and mechanical properties relative to the ambient-air control would falsify the hypothesis.
